speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to prevent the uncalled for defamation of persons or groups on account of race, colour or religion. I would not have brought this matter up, sir, if it had not touched on a very vital and fundamental principle of national life because such defamation, cannot have any other effect than to set up race against race, religious groups against religious groups, and cause unnecessary dissension among the people of this country. subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AT THE DEATH OF HON. WARREN DELANO ROBBINS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AT THE DEATH OF HON. WARREN DELANO ROBBINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure
that this house will consider it fitting that reference should be made to-day to a very unfortunate occurrence, the sudden and untimely death in New York yesterday of the Hon. Warren D. Robbins who was United States Minister to Canada. Mr. Robbins was appointed to this office about two years ago. He had then been a member of the diplomatic service of the United States for some twenty years or more, and had held posts in many places as representative of his country, among others Portugal, France, Berlin and Rome, also Argentina, Chile and Central America. Besides that he had at intervals served the State Department as advisor and delegate at various

international conferences. Mr. Robbins therefore brought to Canada an unusually wide experience of world affairs. He established very friendly relations here, officially and socially, with the people of Ottawa, and he and his wife made for themselves a distinctive place in the life of this country. During these two short years we have reason to appreciate not only his skill and fairness but also the able way in which he put forward the views of his own government, and helped to interpret his country to Canada and also our Canadian views to his own country. He was ill in New York for about a week; this was not supposed to be very serious until Friday or Saturday, and on Saturday night he passed away. He was only in his fiftieth year and therefore might have looked forward to many more years in the service of his country in the career in which he had so distinguished himself.
This government has already sent messages of sympathy to Mrs. Robbins and also to the government of the United States, but as I have said, it seems to me only fitting that we should make reference in this house to-day to this very sad occurrence, and should express our regrets at Mr. Robbins' most untimely and sudden death, and our sympathy with Mrs. Robbins and family. I would therefore ask you, Mr. Speaker, with the consent of the house to convey to Mrs. Robbins our feelings in that regard.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET AT THE DEATH OF HON. WARREN DELANO ROBBINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
may I say that I wholeheartedly agree with the right hon. acting leader of the government in regarding it as most fitting that this house should express its feeling with respect to the untimely and sudden death of Mr. Warren Robbins, the late Minister for the United States at Ottawa. Mr. Robbins' passing constitutes the first break which has been occasioned by death in the diplomatic corps in Ottawa during the eight years of its existence. Although Mr. Robbins had been resident in Ottawa only for .two years, his kindly personality was such that he had come to be known by most of the citizens of the capital, and certainly by all of us who have to do with public affairs, and I am sure his death will be deeply felt very much beyond official circles. I had expected that my right hon. friend would make the felicitous reference he did to the appreciation which the government felt of the manner in which the late minister's official duties were performed. Personally, I, naturally, did not have any official relations with Mr. Robbins, but I was privileged to enjoy a

Reciprocity Negotiations
rather intimate friendship with him, and he always impressed me as a man who had uppermost in his mind the thought of furthering the best of friendly relations between the country which he represented and the country to which he came. He was by no means exclusive in his friendships and sought to have men, to whatever political party they might belong, feel that he was concerned above all else with what might best serve the common interest. As the acting leader of the government has just said, Mr. Robbins might well have looked forward to many years of useful public service. His death will be the more keenly felt not only in that it was so unexpected but because his own country as well as other countries have been robbed of his large experience and helpful spirit in matters pertaining to international affairs.
Personally and on behalf of all hon. members on this side of the house may I say that we would wish to join with hon. gentlemen opposite in having an expression of sympathy of the entire house conveyed to Mrs. Robbins and to the members of the family of the late minister, as well as to his mother, all of whom have been so greatly bereaved. Might I add that I think it would be equally appropriate to extend our expression of sympathy to the President of the United States in the loss he has sustained not only through the death of his representative in this country but in being bereaved of one who was also a relative.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO PROLONGED ADJOURNMENT EXPRESSED IN AMENDMENT TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair I desire to make a few remarks concerning a matter which I believe to be of great importance to this house and to the country, and I intend to conclude with an amendment to the motion. I desire to speak-and I hope it is not too late-on the intimated intention of the government to ask this house to adjourn for the protracted period of five weeks. I believe this suspension is not in the public interest or in the interests of the country, and I wish to give a few reasons for my conviction in that regard.
Everyone will agree, Mr. Speaker, that when parliament is summoned for the dispatch of business it must be kept in session from day to day in a continuous way. I remember having heard! the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) quote Sir Wilfrid Laurier to that effect. A few years ago, the last time a motion of this character was before the house, this question was discussed and I well remember what was then stated by leading members of the house, some of whom are now members of the government and others of whom are still members of the house. I should like to take the liberty of quoting some of the expressions of view then given. There are many members of this house who were also members in 1926, when conditions were of an unusual character. The generai election of 1925 had been inconclusive, due to the fact that the verdict had not been decisive. Neither of the two great parties in Canada had received a majority of the votes, and the balance of power was obviously in the hands of a certain group of independent gentlemen who had been elected either as Progressives, as United Farmers or as Labour members. The government took the only course which was logical and constitutional under the circumstances, and summoned parliament to meet at the earliest possible date after the last writs of the elections had been received.

the same had happened to Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Robert Borden -indeed, to all the great statesmen of Canada.
However, the fact was that he was not in the house. The first business was to decide which party was to form the government of Canada for the period of that parliament. Immediately upon the opening of parliament the question of confidence was put before the House of Commons, the then leader of the ppposition, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, mentioning the fact that nine ministers including the Prime Minister had been defeated. A debate on the subject ensued in an endeavour to ascertain who had the confidence of the majority in the house, and the final division which took place on January 14 revealed by a vote of 123 to 120 that the then government should continue until the end of that parliament.
The following Monday, namely on January 18, the first business which must always be considered, namely the address in reply to the speech from the throne, was moved. The debate on this motion continued until February 1, at which time a division was taken on an amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the opposition. The address was not voted. I notice some hon. members smiling; undoubtedly they will remember the circumstances. On February 2, I moved:
That when this house adjourns immediately after the conclusion of the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, it stand adjourned until March 15, 1926.
I must remind the house that at that time the Prime Minister was in the midst of an election campaign in the constituency of Prince Albert, that there was no minister elected for the province of Ontario, that other ministers had been defeated and that there was a very urgent need and necessity for a reorganization of the government, something which could not be done in the absence of the Prime Minister, or at a time when he was fighting an election in the constituency of Prince Albert. As hon. members will recall, the motion was strenuously opposed. I am not complaining; I am simply relating the facts, and laying before this chamber the doctrine expounded by hon. members then sitting in the house. I have many quotations, but shall refer to only a few of them.

hundred employees, if not more-I do not pretend to give a definite figure, but I know my figure is approximately correct-at work in connection with this machine. Parliament was called, and they are all here. Commitments have been made, and everything is now to stop simply because a moribund government is to try to resuscitate itself.
I shall not quote the observations of the late member for East Algoma, Mr. Nicholson. At page 639 of Hansard the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) is reported as follows:
Now I say again that this government has not the slightest right to ask parliament for an adjournment for even one hour. The business of this country must be looked after. We have a great army of unemployed workingmen who hardly know where they are going to get their daily bread, and if this government remains in power much longer the people will be coming here and praying, not to heaven but to the government: Give us this day our daily bread. This government has proved itself absolutely incapable of carrying on, and' some other government must be put in its place.	_

Just as in this year.

If he cannot answer that question he should not have put those words in the mouth of His Excellency when he met this parliament. They either know or they do not know. Then at page 640 the same hon. member is again reported:

met this parliament, then they have a legislative program ready for this house to consider. If they have no legislative program ready, they should have said so; but if in saying they have a legislative program ready they have deceived us, then I submit they are not entitled to an adjournment under any conditions.
And again at page 642:

If a program is ready-you cannot deny it, because if you do, you have put something in the month of His Excellency that was not true and have deceived the people-if you have the program ready, proceed with it. At page 643 he said:
I ask them (the government) to consider this: In all seriousness do they for a moment think that to ask this house to adjourn for six weeks for the reasons given, under the circumstances stated, is to do other than to bring into still greater contempt than they are now held,_ the institutions under which democracy flourishes in Canada.
My hon,. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) made quite a number of remarks, but I shall give only a few quotations. At page 644 he said:
It raises a very practical issue -with each hon. member in this house. We have come from various parts of Canada, and some of us from very distant parts. We have made our arrangements to remain here during the session of parliament to continue our residence in Ottawa until our parliamentary duties have been performed. Now the government proposes to put us in such a position that we shall have to disrupt these arrangements, make new arrangements at great personal inconvenience, and in many cases at great personal loss.
Then at page 645 of Hansard he said:
Have we not an interest in the matter? I submit wre have. The whole country is watching us to-day; the whole country expects us to continue to perform our duties, to advance and to pass the legislation which the government says it has ready and which it has promised; to bring down to the house.
I have so many quotations here, Mr. Speaker-. I have one from my friend from Mount Royal (Mr. White), a very witty one, but I will pass it over. There are many from

Others who spoke against the adjournment were Mr. Ladner, who is no longer here, Mr. Hocken, Mr. Bristol, Hon. J. W. Edwards, and I must say that some of them were rather vituperative in their language. Here is one from my horn, friend from Marquette (Mr. Mullins) at page 673 of Hansard. He was rather mild. He said:
I know my constituency and western Canada very well, and I know that those who sent us here to carry on the business of this country, and legislate, and legislate quickly, will resent any adjournment of this house.
Then the leader of the opposition of that day, Mr. Meighen, said at page 676 of Hansard:
What is the situation of hon. members here? They have come here and some of them have taken up their abodes for the session. Some have given up their homes. Their families are here. They are to be asked to sit for six weeks in idleness, or to spend it in practically worthless visits to their constituencies. They are asked to do so for no good reason, and for no reason imaginable, except to meet the inconveniences of the 'members1 of the administration brought upon themselves by their own folly. But what are the other reasons? What are the reasons against the adjournment which go deeper than the convenience of hon. members of this house? Is this session a necessary session? The then hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said at page 680 of Hansard:
But the government ask for a blank cheque.
That was a crime then. He went on:
They ask for blind authority from this parliament, without reason, without excuse, to agree to a lengthy adjournment.
Then my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion), who is always very nice in his expression, said at page 728, quoting the English Liberals:
Mr. Gladstone said something along the same lines in -an 'article which he wrote in 1887. He said:	''Individuals may recover from even
serious sickness. It does not appear to be the way with governments/5 It is the opinion of all those whose writings I have had the pleasure of reading that once a government is ill it rarely recovers. This government is seriously ill. It has no more chance of recovery than if it were already dead and buried. In fact, I believe burying is about the only thing that has not been done to it so far.

Then I come to some other reasons why we object to this adjournment. Those were the views expressed at a time when the Prime Minister was unavoidably absent and when many of the ministers could not be present before the reorganization of the cabinet. I call the attention of the house to the fact that at that time there was no legislation which exempted a newly appointed cabinet minister from appearing before his electors for reelection. An appointment of a minister meant a vacancy in the house and I must confess that the majority at that time was not sufficient to permit of many additional vacancies. These reasons were given day in and day out before the vote was taken. An amendment was moved by the then member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), seconded by the present acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) and reading as follows:
This house having been called in session at the instance of the present government, and a number of legislative and other proposals submitted for its consideration by said government in the form of a speech from the throne, it is the duty of the house, should the address in reply to the speech from the throne be adopted, to proceed with the public business until same is disposed of

The vote was taken on February 5 and the motion to adjourn was carried by a vote of 120 to 112, a majority of eight. Immediately afterwards, on February 8, the debate on the address resumed. Other amendments were moved because the adjournment was to take place only after the address had been debated. The debate continued until February 16, when the then hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) moved the previous question in order to preclude more amendments being moved to the address. The address continued until March 1 when I was compelled to give notice that on the following date the debate would not be further adjourned. On March 2 the motion of the then hon. member for Nelson was voted
upon and the address in reply was also voted upon. This meant that the house would adjourn until March 15 but this vote took place exactly one month after the motion for adjournment had carried. The adjournment was only for thirteen days because of these tactics. During all this time the house was not transacting necessary business, all that occurred was a discussion of futile political matters to prevent the adjournment of the house. The will of the majority of this house was thwarted because there had been a majority vote on March 2 for adjournment. On March 15 the house resumed its work and my right hon. friend took his seat. That was one of the best times in my life because I was only too glad to hand over to him the work I had had to do during those hectic times. He then began the reorganization of the cabinet.
How can those hon. gentlemen who took such a firm stand at that time against adjournment ask us to vote at the present time for an adjournment of five weeks? This is the sixth session of this parliament and ordinarly it should have ended last year. Only twice has a Canadian parliament gone the full limit of its time. We were told the other day that the life of this parliament will end on August 18 but as a matter of fact it has already gone beyond the time normally given to parliaments.

speechtext:
It would be useless to
discuss this with my hon. friend.
Not only have we reached the limit of the life of this parliament but the people of the country have expressed in an emphatic way a lack of confidence in the present government. It is a well known maxim of representative government under British rules that the government must possess the confidence of the country as well as of parliament. I quoted authorities to that effect. I should like to refer to the expressions of opinion which have been given by the people of Canada during the last two years. There was a by-election in South Huron on September 26, 1932, and the Liberal majority was increased from 349 to 1989. There was a byelection in Yamaska, on October 23, 1933, when the old Liberal majority of one was increased to 84. This is not a large increase but the present majority is 84 times that of the old majority. At the by-election held in Mackenzie, on October 23, 1933, the previous Independent majority of 3,076 was changed to a Liberal majority of, 1,614. In the byelection held in Restigouche-Madawaska on

Long Adjournment-Mr. Lapointe
the same date, the previous Conservative majority of 548 was changed to a Liberal majority of 6,472. In the by-election held in South Oxford on April 16, 1934, the previous Liberal majority of 55 was increased to 1,493. In the by-election held on September 24, 1934 in West Elgin the previous Liberal majority of 1,437 was increased to 2,493. In the by-election held in Frontenac-Addington on the same date the previous Conservative majority of 3,371 was changed to a Liberal majority of 2,651. In Kenora-Rainy River cm the same day the Liberal majority was increased from 502 to 6,165. In North York a Conservative majority of 298 was changed into a Liberal majority of 3,687. In East Toronto the Conservative majority at the last election was 7,075. The present member won a personal victory, but he had 2,143 fewer votes than the Liberal and Cooperative Commonwealth Federation candidates combined.
In every provincial election which has taken place during those two years the Liberal party has been returned to power, winning a decisive victoiy, and in every one of those provincial campaigns federal issues were generously discussed. Indeed I heard at eleven or twelve o'clock in the evening on the eve of the general election in Ontario the speech of the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in a slumber hour address to the electors of that province asking them to elect Mr. Henry. It is impossible to deny the fact that the Conservative party-and I am .sorry for many of my hon. friends opposite-has been shattered and has suffered the most humiliating defeat in its history. Popular discontent has started to grow into a blizzard. They have decided-and of course that was their business -to remain in office in the hope of some miracle happening before the end of their term to prevent their complete destruction. That is a policy of fear and distrust of the people. It looks as if my hon. friends opposite were shivering on the brink.
In this parliament vacancies have occurred which have not been filled. This session is supposed 'to be a most important one when a whole new program of social reform is to be put into effect and the necessary legislation enacted. Have the electors in those constituencies not a right to be represented in this house while this program is being discussed? In Halifax and Long Lake notice of the vacancies were signed on October 9, 1934; if I mistake not, that will be six months tomorrow. In St. Denis the notice was signed on October 30, 1934, and in East Algoma notice was signed on January 4 of this year.

I shall not refer to the vacancy which occurred recently in Montmagny. There is a vacancy also in Saint John, but it happened during this session, but the first three vacancies I mentioned occurred in the course of last autumn. Surely in an ordinary parliament, a government administering the affairs of the country in normal circumstances and not afraid of going before its judges, could have issued the writs and permitted those constituencies to be represented. Under such conditions I claim that this parliament has no moral jurisdiction for legislating.
This so-called social reform program has been propounded in the shadow of an impending election. The old order has gone, as we were told over the air and in the house. I admit the old order has gone as far as parliamentary government and constitutional practice are concerned. We had the speech from the throne on January 17, and I shall now refer to the program placed before the house in that speech and ask hon'. members how that program has been fulfilled, and whether we have a right to go home for five weeks when the greater part of this program has not even been considered. I read this in the speech from the throne;
Reform measures will therefore be submitted to you as part of a comprehensive plan designed to remedy the social and economic injustices now prevailing, and to ensure to all classes and to all parts of the country a greater degree of equality in the distribution of the benefits of the capitalist system.
How this has been done., I fail to see. Second:
Better provision will be made for the security of the worker during unemployment, in sickness, and in old age.
What has been done under this plan? We have had a bill to provide for unemployment insurance. This bill is still before the Senate and important witnesses are being heard before its committee on banking and commerce. We do not know whether the bill will bo changed there and whether we shall not have to work on it again when it oomes back from the other house. That is for unemployment insurance, but has anything been done for the security of the worker in sickness, as was stated in the speech from the throne would be done? Nothing at all, except the commissioners for unemployment insurance will have a right to inquire into the conditions of public health in Canada. As regards old age, nothing at all has come before us. Surely if the government is going to proceed with legislation affecting these various subjects, we

______ Long Adjournment-Mr. Lapointe
should have such measures before us and consider them instead of going home for five weeks.
Again I quote from the speech from the throne:
Action will be taken to ameliorate the conditions of labour, to provide a better and more assured standard of living for the worker, to secure minimum wages and a maximum working week, and to alter the incidence of taxation so that it will more directly conform to capacity to pay.
With regard to ameliorating the conditions *of labour, what has been done? The eight hour day bill is I understand also before the Senate and they are hearing witnesses before one of their committees. Even this eight hour day bill is not I think very satisfactory to labour in Canada. The bill to secure minimum wages and a maximum working hour is still on the order paper for second reading. Why should it niot be moved in the house so as to let us deal with this matter instead of adjourning for five weeks?
As regards the phrase:
_ To alter the incidence of taxation so that it will more directly conform to the capacity to pay.
What does that mean? The changes in the budget? I fail to see that they are altering the incidence of taxation in order to help those who cannot pay. However those changes are before the house and they have not yet been touched. We have not so far considered them and before we are asked to study the various changes of taxation, we are asked to go home for five weeks.
Again, the speech from the throne states:
You will be invited to enact measures designed to safeguard the consumer and primary producer against unfair trading practices and to regulate, in the public interest, concentrations in production and distribution.
That no doubt refers to the price spreads committee, and I do not see why the house should adjourn in order that legislation may be prepared resulting from the work of that committee. Every session we have important committees sitting on important matters, and legislation is prepared during the session while other business is before the house and while members of parliament are proceeding with their work.
The speech from the throne continues:
You will be invited also to enact measures to provide the investing public with means to protect itself against exploitation.
Well, we have been told that there would be a bill to make unlawful the issue of no par shares, but this has not been done so far. If the government is going to do it why not do it? Why not introduce legislation to that 92582-160
effect and let the members of parliament work on that legislation instead of going home for five weeks?
The speech from the throne proceeds:
My government has under consideration the adoption, throughout the penitentiaries of Canada, of a system similar to that which is known in England as the Borstal system, and is making investigations as to its operation.
My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) said when his estimates were before the committee last Thursday that he has that in mind, that it is his intention to establish this system, but that there are technical matters to consider and that he is going to send the superintendent of penitentiaries to the old country for the purpose of making inquiry as to how the system works there, which means further delay. Why not proceed with this thing, or why not have proceeded earlier? The chances are that even with the adjournment of five weeks it will not be ready until the next session.

speechtext:
The speech from the
throne continues:
My ministers have under consideration a plan for the reorganization of the government services so that they may be better equipped to discharge the onerous duties which devolve upon them. You will be invited to consider measures, the purpose of which will be to authorize the first stage in this plan of reorganization.
Well, nothing has been done so far as this new coordination of departments is concerned. If it is to be done, surely in the language of the Prime Minister when he was member

Long Adjournment-Mr. Lapointe
for Calgary in 1926, why put it in the mouth of His Excellency if it is not to be done, and if it is to be done, why not do it instead of sending us home for five weeks?
As to the economic council, there was legislation as far as that goes.
Then we have other legislation on the order paper. There is one very important piece of legislation:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to establish a board to be known as the Canadian grain board with power to purchase, receive and take delivery of wheat, oats, barley, rye and flax-seed, or any one or more of such grains for marketing and to sell, store, transport and market such grains, and to provide for the appointment of such clerks, employees and assistants as may be necessary, and to provide for their remuneration and for the expenses of, and arising out of, the operations of the board.
This notice was given a long time ago, why has nothing been done in that respect? The grain producers and the grain trade are all anxious to know what is going to happen. The taxpayers of Canada, not only in the west but in the east also, are anxious to know the results of the operations of this mystery man, Mr. McFarland. I find it rather queer that while this thing is not discussed in parliament, when you open the morning papers, as we did this morning, we read an interview with this Mr. McFarland saying what he is doing and what he is going to do with the wheat of the west. I think that should be said in the parliament of Canada; it should be discussed here instead of in the newspapers. There is also the Canadian farm loan bill which is still in the Senate, where they hear witnesses in regard to it, and we do not know in what shape or form it will come back when it does come back.
I have related the work that has been done, or rather the work that has not been done. I claim, sir, that it is an extraordinary presumption on the part of the government to ask for an adjournment of this house under those conditions, and it would be extreme simplicity on our part to agree to an adjournment under these conditions. In the country there is anger and impatience; unemployment is raging. Is it fair to ask us to suspend the work of parliament for five weeks while there is such distress in Canada, and without any definite program of public works or of unemployment relief proposed for the consideration of parliament? If the government has a plan let them give it to this house. We are not living in an age in which mystery men can long hide their trick boxes. All we have had is a patchwork quilt of paternalistic proposals and a conglomeration of half-baked

measures. Our attitude the government surely cannot complain of, we on this side have exercised great restaint even under provocation. Nothing has stood in the way of the government's measures except the uncertain and doubtful validity of their methods.
Take the budget debate; my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has delivered his budget. There has been a discussion on it in which twenty-two Conservative speakers were heard besides the Minister of Finance, and they used fourteen hours and forty minutes of the time of parliament. The hon. gentlemen to my left had five speakers who used three hours and ten minutes. speechtext:
No, I am very much
alive, I shall prove it when the time comes. I am pleased that the acting leader of the house did not give as a justification for this adjournment the trip of the Prime Minister. We all regret his illness, and we hope that this trip will help him to recover fully. But that is no reason why the house could not and should not proceed. I am pleased also that the presence of the Prime Minister in London is to be rather a social function and that there will be no formal conference as in 1911 and 1917, when the Prime Minister had to go as an ex-officio member of the imperial conference, which has become a permanent institution. We were told by the acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) that nothing would take place except informal conversations. I was glad to hear that statement, because there have been rather alarming reports to the contrary. The Round Table, which as everyone knows is a leading, well informed periodical in connection with imperial matters, in its

Long Adjournment-Mr. Lapointe
issue of March, 1935, at page 217 in an article headed The Commonwealth and the World, had this to say:
The _ gathering of empire prime ministers which is to take place this spring in connection with the jubilee of the Kings accession to the throne will be the most important imperial conference since 1926. That conference laid down the principles upon which the British commonwealth itself was to rest. The forthcoming meeting, though not technically an imperial conference, will be called upon to lay down the basis for the future foreign policy of the commonwealth in the very changed conditions that have come into being in the last nine years.
Further it says:
It is quite clear that decisions of the utmost gravity, affecting the policy to which both Great Britain and the dominions are to commit themselves in Europe, in the Pacific, and towards the collective system generally, will have to be taken in the near future. More than ever the British commonwealth is the chief unifying and stabilizing factor in the world. But it will only maintain that position if its members are agreed among themselves both about the facts with which they have to deal and the policy which they will jointly pursue.
Obviously those gentlemen were wrong, and I am very glad to accept the statement of my right hon. friend that nothing of the kind will happen. It would not be fair, especially to Canada under the present circumstances, because we on this side of the house and many people throughout the country believe the present government have not the right to speak for Canada on matters of such importance.
I have another question on which I should like to say a word, in connection with this celebration. There has been a report which has come to my ears, at all events, to the effect that advantage will be taken of this celebration to distribute many new titles of honour to Canadian citizens. I hope that will not be the case. Last year the house divided on this question and the Liberal party unanimously, the independents and even some of the Conservative members voted against this institution of titles in Canada. I claim that under the circumstances a title is only a Conservative badge, because the Liberals and other parties are opposed to them. It is not fair to the crown to advise the continuation of an institution which is obnoxious and abhorrent to a large majority of the Canadian people, especially when it is supported by a government which no longer has the right to speak for the Canadian people. Only last week we saw the effect of titles on the mentality of a man. After the name of the new governor general was announced, a gentleman who was on the last 92582-1604
list of honours gave an interview to the Toronto newspapers in which he said he had never heard of the man, and apart from that he was in favour of members of the nobility being appointed governors general of Canada. I am sure this gentleman was bom an ordinary Canadian citizen with a sound mind, but I am afraid the fact that he has been given a title has brought chaos to his brain and mentality. We do not want that sort of thing, and the sooner it is done away with the better.
In that connection I should like to make a suggestion. It is sometimes said that we who take this stand on this question perhaps do not represent the majority of the people, and that we have not the right to say that the people think as we do. There is a very easy way to consult the people and find out for all time what Canadians want in that regard. We are going to have a general election this summer. Why not take a referendum at the same time and ask every voter in Canada whether or not he is in favour of titles? That will not cost anything and it will decide the matter.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I claim that this parliament should be sitting during the jubilee festivities, as the imperial parliament will be sitting. His Majesty will even go to the imperial parliament to receive the address which will be voted by the House of Commons and the House of Lords. Could we not have the same celebration here, with an address to the crown, with parliament sitting? The place of members of parliament during this celebration is in Ottawa. Every member of parliament should take part in the official functions which will take place in Ottawa on May 6, and parliament should be sitting here at that time. Last week a leading newspaper, and a Conservative newspaper at that, discussing this proposed adjournment said that public interest must be the only consideration for parliament in the decision of this matter. It is this consideration of public interest that actuates me m moving, seconded by the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff).
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be omitted, and the following substituted therefor:
Whereas this seventeenth parliament has held five sessions -and is now concluding a sixth session;
And whereas the limit of five years fixed by the constitution as that beyond which a parliament cannot legally continue in existence will very shortly be reached, and parliament itself will be legally dissolved by constitutional limitation of time;
And whereas certain measures suggested iD the speech from the throne at the opening of parliament on January 17 have not yet been considered or introduced;

Long Adjournment-Mr. Guthrie
. And whereas it is obviously desirable that the time of the general elections should not be delayed beyond that which will permit of parliament duly concluding its sessional program;
Therefore be it resolved that this house is 'of the opinion that a period of adjournment at the Easter season beyond one week is not desirable, and that save for such brief and customary adjournment the public interest will be best served by parliament continuing in session until it has completed:
(1)	the consideration of those measures mentioned in the speech from the throne and not yet introduced;
(2)	the completion of the discussion of the measures already before the house and not yet passed;
(3)	the consideration of such legislative proposals as may be rendered necessary or advisable by the report of the price spreads commission :and the report of the special committee on housing.
. Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Minister of Justice) :	Mr. Speaker, we have just listened
with pleasure to a very long and interesting -discussion of a great variety of matters by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). Many of the matters upon which he touched were entirely apart from the motion he has seen fit to move. Certainly the hon. member has given us an historical resume of political events in this chamber during the rather hectic session of 1926.
Many will remember that nine years ago a rather odd situation developed in our parliamentary history, but I assert that that situation affords a very slight parallel, if any, to the situation now existing in this chamber. The session of 1926 opened under a government which had been practically slaught-. ered at the polls, and but for a crooked count : and also some ballot box manipulations in the northwestern part of Canada the government would have come to parliament in an gctual minority. The Prime Minister had been defeated by the constituents in his own riding, nine of his ministers had gone down -to defeat, and the great province of Ontario .was not represented in the House of Com, mons by a single minister. Under those circumstances any self-respecting government-.would have taken the course the people of Canada desired it to take, but the then government did not see fit to follow that course. They realized after the first vote in this house which indicated a majority of only two-
,[DOT] Mr. LAPOINTE: Three.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
-a majority of three, that they were practically defeated. They -could not elect new ministers, they had only the tag end of a government in the chamber and had no Prime Minister entitled to . take his seat. Still they persisted in holding on and continuing in office. What did they suggest? Under conditions such as I

have just pictured they solemnly moved in this chamber that the house stand adjourned for six weeks merely for their own convenience. Now hon. members opposite strenuously object to a proposal to adjourn the House of Commons four or five weeks, despite the fact that the government can give good and substantial reasons for its request.
All the quotations made by my hon. friend this afternoon from speeches made in parliament nine years ago, while perhaps interesting as political history, have no application whatsoever to the situation with which we are confronted to-day. Let us take a practical view of what the situation really is at the present time. My hon. friend suggests, and correctly so, that in the speech from the throne certain legislation was forecast for the present session. The most important legislation forecast was of a remedial or reform order, and largely dependent upon the report of a single commission known as the price spreads commission, previously a committee of this house. Hon. members opposite state that in former years committees of the house have sat for long periods, have reported and that during the same session legislation has been framed following their reports. I say to hon. members opposite that never in the history of the parliament of Canada have we had a commission which sat practically throughout the whole of the last session and which has continued as a royal commission to sit from the end of last session to the present moment and as yet has not reported. The commission has heard thousands and thousands of pages of evidence and, according to the newspapers, has produced a report about 250 pages in length, which report discusses some of the most important problems before the people of Canada to-day, and makes some of the most important suggestions for the most difficult and involved legislation which has in the past been or will in the future be placed before the parliament of Canada..
This is the eighth day of April. Ordinarily when Easter has intervened there has been a parliamentary recess varying from one week to two weeks; that has been my experience throughout many sessions. So that under ordinary circumstances, with no abnormal conditions, on the 18th or 19th of April next we might expect an adjournment of a week, ten days or two weeks. That would have been the case, even if there had been no report from the price spreads commission.
Having regard to the situation actually confronting us the government proposes an adjournment two or two and one-half weeks longer than the usual Easter recess. As a

Long Adjournment-Mr. Guthrie
ground for our request we ask the house seriously to consider the legislation we have yet to prepare and pass through the house.
I submit that legislation could not fairly be drafted and considered under two or three weeks. I know something whereof I speak, so far as the preparation of involved and intricate bills is concerned, because I am sorry to say many difficult bills have to be prepared in the Department of Justice. Two or three weeks time would be required to prepare the necessary legislation, and the work of drafting cannot be begun until the report, which up to the present time is not before us, has been thoroughly considered. If that alone were the reason for asking the adjournment I submit our grounds would be sufficient to warrant an adjournment to May 20.
But there are additional reasons, as every person knows, for asking a longer adjournment at this time. One reason is that the head of this government, the Prime Minister of Canada, the minister who has taken the most active interest- in the whole sessional program thus far presented and who will be mainly responsible for the program afterwards to be presented, will be absent from Canada until May 18 or 20. He is the head of the government; he is the first minister of the crown; he is the leader of the House of Commons, and I submit it is not only7 essential but absolutely necessary that he be present in this chamber to guide our deliberations when these important measures are introduced and carried through the house. Would any person suggest for one moment that the Prime Minister should continue his duties here rather than attend the silver jubilee in England? I submit any proposal of that kind would receive absolutely no support either in this chamber or throughout the country. He is bound to go to England; it is his duty to go; it is his privilege to go, and it would be a tremendous disappointment to the Canadian people were he not present on that wonderful occasion. If I am correctly informed-and I believe I am -the hon. member for Quebec East need not worry about imperial conferences which are going to take place in London or which would bind Canada in the future. My hon. friend need not pay much attention to the Round Table article which he read to the house. It has been stated in this chamber by the acting Prime Minister that there will only be informal conversations between the Prime Ministers of the self-governing dominions and the members of the British government. It is very fitting and proper that these conversations should take place, and it would be better in my judgment if they took place more frequently than they do.
In our parliamentary history there is an exact parallel for the present situation, an-excellent parallel but one that my hon. friend-hardly mentioned in his remarks this afternoon. He was a member in this chamber in the year 1911, so was I. There was a corona-' tion ceremony to take place in London in 1911.	The	coronation	was to	take place inGreat	Britain in the	month	of June, andhis present	Majesty	was to	be crowned.There was also preliminary and concurrent with that event an imperial conference. The' Prime Minister of Canada was not only-invited to the conference but invited also to the coronation. I had the honour of being present at the coronation as one of the delegates	from	Canada.	I think	that SenatorBeland and Senator Casgrain of the upper house and mj'self are probably the only ones of that delegation still remaining in public life, although I am not quite sure. I remember the pride we felt as the Prime Minister of Canada walked down the aisle of Westminster Abbey, the great representative of-this country on that important occasion, and I rejoice to know that our present Prime Minister will be present on the twenty-fifth anniversary of the reign of that same monarch. When the question was raised in parliament in the session of 1911, Sir Robert Borden, then Mr. Robert Borden, was the leader of the opposition, and what was his attitude in regard to the matter? What did Sir Wilfred Laurier request? An adjournment of four or five weeks? No, an adjournment of two months in the middle of the session. The adjournment was granted, on the nineteenth of May, and ex-, tended to the eighteenth of July. Was there any question of not granting one or, two month's supply on that occasion? No,, supply was readily voted. The way was-cleared, and the Prime Minister of Canada attended the conference and attended the coronation, and parliament stood adjourned for two straight months save one day. Such was the attitude of the leader of the opposition in the then House of Commons. Mr. Robert Borden on that occasion expressed his pleasure and delight to concur in the proposal to grant Sir Wilfred Laurier the adjournment of two months which he requested. I have his language on that occasion before me now. Mr. Robert Borden, on the motion to adjourn, said at page 8712 of the Hansard of 1911:	'
In conclusion I can only say that I am very-happy indeed that the Prime Minister will he able to attend, both the imperial conference and the coronation.

Long Adjournment-Mr. Guthrie
And he did not divide the house upon the motion to grant a two months' adjournment. My hon. friend has endeavoured to cite precedents. This parliament by law certainly continues until the eighteenth of August. I know that there is a rather nice legal question whether it does not perhaps continue for a longer period until the date the last of the election writs was returned, but I can only repeat what I answered to my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition a day or two ago in reply to his question, that it has been the invariable practice to treat the date mentioned in the proclamation of the election for the return of the writs as the actual expiring date of that parliament. Parliament can legally exist certainly until the eighteenth of August. Oh but, my hon. friend from Quebec says, that such has not been the custom in the past. Well, it has been merely a question of the whim of the then government or of the then Prime Minister. I remember a very prominent Liberal chieftain in this country who said to me one day, "Guthrie, the time to go to the country is when you can win." That I think has been the guiding principle at every dissolution, and it is because we think we can win, that we are going in due time to the electors.

speechtext:
Oh yes, we will have an
election and we will be on this side of the house when the election is over.
What I submit, Mr. Speaker, is that we have made a reasonable and a proper request for an adjournment. I am not going to deal with many of the questions mentioned by my hon. friend from Quebec East. He mentioned the budget and the time it occupied in this house. We are all glad that the budget did not occupy much time but the budget did not lend itself to adverse criticism.
I notice that my hon. friend also touched upon the Borstal system and some other matters mentioned in the speech from the throne. But the real ground for this adjournment, Mr. Speaker, is the preparation of necessary legislation as a consequence of the report of the price spreads commission, expected this week. Any man that says he can deal within two or three weeks with the price spreads report, and the important questions which the commission has considered and developed, does not know the task he has ahead of him. We expect when we come back in May that all such legislation will be

ready, and what is more, we feel confident that the Prime Minister will be in his place to direct the proceedings of the house.
I am very glad to conclude these remarks by quoting the support of the Toronto Globe for this proposal as it appears in an editorial in the issue of to-day. The Globe says:
Liberals and independent members have protested against the long suspension of the sittings, and in some of their contentions there is much logic. Nevertheless, the unusual length of the recess will not be without its all-round advantages. Most Canadians will feel that it is eminently desirable that the dominion shall be represented by its Prime Minister at the Ring s jubilee ceremonies in London on May 6. There will be general rejoicing at the news conveyed by Sir George Perley that the improvement m Mr. Bennett's condition justifies every hope that he will be well enough to make the overseas journey and take his part in the festivities.
True, it might have been possible, as the opposition leader suggested, to proceed with business in the Prime Minister's absence under arrangements which would permit Mr. Bennett to be present before prorogation. But, as the acting Prime Minister intimated, there is much to be done in the preparation of legislation, especially that proceeding from the price spreads and housing reports.
Time and thought will be required in the framing of legislation which seeks to set right the many economic and social injustices revealed in the voluminous reports. It will be in the public interest that action shall not be hasty and ill considered, but rather that it shail represent judgments reached after earnest study and proper correlation of details.
These are very sound reasons for granting this adjournment, supported by the leading Liberal organ in the province of Ontario and probably in the whole dominion. Such is the case which I have been endeavouring to make, made probably far better by the Globe than any language of mine could make it. I appeal to hon. members in every part of the house that the proposal to adjourn is reasonable, it is practical, it is businesslike. It is what any government, I care not what government might be in power, would offer under similar circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to my mind the amendment moved by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) is the most important which has been moved in this house during the twenty sessions I have had the honour of attending this parliament. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson) was able to accept the present position *which he occupies without appealing to his constituents. He has referred to this amendment as a sham but let me say to him that there are hon. members in this house and

Long Adjournment-Mr. Duff
people in this country who have just as good an idea of the conditions in this country as he has. I do not think it becomes one of His Majesty's privy councillors to make such a remark. If we are going to talk about shams we do not need to look to this side of the house or to hon. members on this side who feel that they should either move such an amendment or do as I have done, second it. Let me say to my hon. friend that when the people of this country read of this amendment in tomorrow's papers they will not consider it a sham. Many of these people have already come to the conclusion that this is a government of sham and camouflage and they will consider a motion to adjourn this house for six weeks as nothing more than a sham. I intend to try to show that there is no necessity for such an adjournment.
Because the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) wants to attend the jubilee celebration is no reason why this house should be adjourned. We all sincerely regret that because of hard work the Prime Minister has been laid up on a sick bed for a number of weeks, but we have not been going around the country, as was done last year, to tell of the terrible physical condition of certain public men. I believe I voice the sentiment of all hon. members when I say I regret exceedingly that the Prime Minister has been ill. We on this side of the house want him to get well; the people of the country want him to get well. We want the Prime Minister to be able to lead his party whether it appeals to the country tomorrow or at the eleventh hour of the last day they can hold on to office. That is our position with regard to the Prime Minister.
I believe I have some idea of what the business people of this country are thinking. They want this government to go on with the business of parliament so that the session can be concluded as quickly as possible. My hon. friend read an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Globe. That newspaper is generally considered as being a Liberal newspaper but my opinion gained from a reading of it for a number of years is that it is independent. I should like to quote from an interview given by the gentleman who owns the Truro News, a Conservative paper.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
I do not know why my hon.
friends should laugh because there is no question but that the proprietor of this newspaper is a Conservative. The article reads:
A. R. Coffin returned to Truro Friday from a two weeks' business trip to Montreal, New York and Philadelphia.
It concludes:
Speaking with the editor Mr. Coffin expressed the opinion that business in Canada shows an indication to slow up until after the general election and until the question of governmental policy is definitely settled so that industrialists in particular can feel safe to take the road forward.
The business people of this country want us to stay here until the business is completed, no matter how long or short a period it may take. Let me tell the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) that we are not acting as the opposition did in 1926 and at other sessions. We realize that the quicker this legislation is passed the better it will be. The legislation suggested by the bedtime stories the Prime Minister told in January should be brought down and passed so that this government may have the full responsibility of such legislation. They can then appeal to the country and let the people decide whether or not they are in favour of returning this government to power.
The proposal for this adjournment has given us an opportunity to judge just what kind of a government we have on the treasury benches. They came to us a few days ago and suggested an adjournment but they did not know the exact date on which the adjournment was to commence. The acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) has said that he is willing to leave it to us to decide when we shall go home before Easter. He has not named the exact date for the adjournment as has always been done. This shows that the government does not know what they should do. As I said a moment ago, we all regret the illness of the Prime Minister but is it fair that 244 members of this House of Commons and 86 members of the Senate should have to leave here with our business incomplete to go home for six weeks and then return on the 20th May because of that illness? We will all be put to great expense and inconvenience. The public affairs of the country should not be treated in that way. Apparently there has been considerable criticism of this proposed long adjournment and the other day my right hon. friend threw out a sop to the members of parliament when he said that they would receive their travelling expenses to and from their homes. I say to him that that should not be necessary. After all, the taxpayers of this country will have to pay this money. Because one man is not able to attend to his parliamentary duties, the taxpayers of the country must pay the travelling expenses of 244 members of the House of Commons and 86 senators
Long Adjournment-Mr. Duff

The announcement is made to-day by the acting Prime Minister that the employees attached to the House of Commons and the Senate will be paid their salaries during this six weeks adjournment. I am in favour of paying good wages as I believe the labourer is worthy of his hire but I say to the acting Prime Minister and the ministers who sit behind him that they have no right to take the people's money to pay these employees for six weeks. These employees will not be doing anything and it is not necessary. The fact that this statement has been made is not going to settle this matter in the minds of the electors of the country.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO PROLONGED ADJOURNMENT EXPRESSED IN AMENDMENT TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is the fair thing to do.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO PROLONGED ADJOURNMENT EXPRESSED IN AMENDMENT TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes, it is the fair thing to do; but if anybody is going to pay those sessional employees, it is the members in the house who will vote against the amendment and the members of the government which is asking for this adjournment, who should pay, and not the taxpayers, 700,000 of whom are out of employment while the rest are struggling along the best way they can. If my hon. friend) and his colleagues want to pay those employees, well and good; I have no objection to that, but the government has no right to take the taxpayers' money in order to pay the stenographers, sessional clerks and everybody else for the next six weeks while this adjournment is in progress.
We had a very interesting discussion of this matter by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie). He rather laughingly suggested that we should not go back to the days of 1926 and read in the house statements made by him and others during that period. However history has a way of repeating itself, and sometimes we cannot do better than go back in history in order to discuss certain matters in connection with public affairs or anything else. He said that there was no parallel between what is happening to-day and the reason for asking this adjournment and the situation in 1926. The Minister of Justice is quite correct and I agree with him, but the situation to-day is greately exaggerated in comparison with what it was in 1926. It is true that in that year we had a certain political issue that was not settled perhaps as well as it might have been, but the economic condition then was entirely different from what it is to-day. People throughout this country, men in employment, men in business are anxious that this government should bring down all its legislation and should appeal to the electorate at the earliest possible moment. (Mr. Duff.]
So I say to the Minister of Justice that there is no parallel between financial and economic conditions in 1926 and to-day.
My hon. friend also referred to the fact that in 1926 the then government did not have very many ministems elected, and he told us that in Ontario no ministers were elected. As I said a moment ago, the only way in which this government can appoint ministers is by act of parliament; now that the act has been changed, they do not have to go to the country. But even in the constituency of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hanson), if he had had to appeal to his constituents for reeleetion, I have no hesitation in saying that there would be a great difference between the vote he received in 1930 and the one he is likely to get in the next general election. Therefore, while those ministers were defeated at that time, I have no doubt the same fate will overtake many ministers of *this government. We must not forget also that the Canadian people have spoken in every by-election. They did not have a chance in connection with ministers, but whenever they had a chance, they voted against the government with very large majorities.
I do not know whether the Minister of Justice or I should discuss the matter of the price spreads commission, but perhaps I may say just a word. I agree with him that this commission has laboured strenuously for more than a year, and I understand it has cost the country some $560,000. I have not seen the report and I do not know who is giving out the information. The ex-Miaister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) has of course on platforms and in pulpits been giving out information as to what the commission should or should not do and so forth. As to whether this was -the proper way to proceed or not I have no hesitation in saying it was against all parliamentary usage. This is the first time in the history of the country that the report of a commission before being brought down, has been made the subject of broadcasts throughout the dominion and speculation as to what it is likely to contain. The newspapers must have got their information somewhere, and from press reports it looks to me, if I may say so without offence, that the mountain has laboured and brought forth a mouse. After spending $560,000; after bringing auditors from all over Canada to go into the books of different concerns; after bringing witnesses from all parts of the dominion and after paying special investigators huge sums of money, what does this report in the newspapers tell us? Practically all this commission asks the government or parliament to do is

Long Adjournment-Mr. Duff
to appoint seven or eight other commissions. In other words, we are to appoint seven or eight other commissions to look into the business of the Canadian people. We are going to have, I suppose, doctors, lawyers, professors and everybody else trying to run the business of the country by different commissions as is being done under the so-called Marketing Act instead of men trained in various industries. If that is the only suggestion this commission can make, then they have not dealt properly with the price spreads investigation. However I am willing to wait for the report; perhaps after all there may be something good in it. But I do not agree with the government that it is necessary to have a six weeks' adjournment m order to give them time to consider the report of the price spreads commission. Of course in this country under our democratic system there are certain things which are kept secret. For instance the meetings of the cabinet are not supposed to go out to the public; meetings of commissions in camera are not supposed to be made public; but you, sir, will agree with me when I say that t-he government, not to-day, not last week but for perhaps weeks or months have known from time to time what this commission had in their minds and what they were going to report. So there was no difficulty in my hon. friends, who sit on the treasury benches, the members of the government, drafting certain legislation with regard to the report which the price spreads commission will make. If I am not mistaken, the Prime Minister in those wonderful fairy tales which he gave us over the radio in January referred to the legislation which would be brought down in connection with the price spreads investigation. He had advance information, and if he knew practically what should be done, why should we wait not only from January to April before the government is ready with its legislation but for another six weeks?
While we regret the Prime Minister's absence, I think I may say without offence that we have no guarantee that he will be able to return to parliament by May 20 even after a long adjournment, although of course we all hope he will get back. I want to say this to the acting leader of the government, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Postmaster General and other members of this government: Under the circumstances you are not doing so badly. We have treated you pretty decently and fairly; we have helped you with the legislation; we have not held up any. If we had held up legislation; if we had fought every item introduced by the government for a week or ten days or longer as my hon. friends across the floor did in 1926,
there might be some cause for complaint. But we have helped the acting leader of the government, and in the interests of the country, seeing that he has done fairly well under the circumstances, he should carry on, bring down the legislation and deal with it. If we are to adjourn, we should adjourn from Thursday of holy week until the following Tuesday when we should proceed to deal with the public business no matter how long or short a time this may take. But it is not in the interests of the taxpayers and the business men who are waiting for some lead from somebody, from either this government or a new one, that we should have this long adjournment at this time. If there is anything in my hon. friend's argument that the reason for this adjournment is that they want the Prime Minister to go to the jubilee celebrations and also that they are embarrassed by his absence, as I assume they are to a certain extent, why did not my right hon, friend ask for an adjournment some eight weeks ago? From the bulletins which were being issued and the statements of the doctor regarding the Prime Minister's health the acting Prime Minister several weeks ago, must have known that the Prime Minister could not come back to this house for six or eight or ben weeks. That was the time to ask for an adjournment, if he and his colleagues could not get along without the Prime Minister. But why ask for it now, when the Prime Minister is getting better and the government is getting along fairly well with its legislation? Why send 244 members of parliament and 84 senators back to their homes and disrupt the whole business of parliament and of people who have business to do in this country?
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) made another excuse for the long adjournment. He said: If we adjourn now we would get through the business of the house and there would likely be very great criticism in the country because the government would not appeal to the people within a short time after the house prorogued. He said that the time to go to the country is when you can win. Well, that is an intimation to the people of the country that the Minister of Justice and bis colleagues-because I assume he was speaking for them-realize that they dare not face the people now. They have to wait until the last minute of the eleventh hour, but they will find it will make no difference no matter when they dissolve this house. It is most unfair. We shall find that the writs will be issued at the very last minute, and the people will be given a chance to defeat this government only at the very last day that the election can possibly be held.

Long Adjournment-Mr. Duff
The Minister of Justice also said that the reason that we on this side did not criticize the budget or speak against it was that it was not open to criticism. Well, Mr. Speaker, I think everyone will admit that there was not much in the budget except the figures, and the financial statement gives perhaps the correct figures of the financial standing of the country but even then it is nothing to write home about. We did not criticize the budget-why? Because it is a diabetic budget. We had a diabetic budget two years ago when there was a tax of two cents a pound put on the poor people's sugar, and this year they bring in another diabetic budget. Last year they reduced the special tax on sugar to one cent a pound, this year they did not take off that one cent, but they took the duty off biscuits which are used for people who have Bright's disease. That is the kind of budget they give us.
It seems to me, sir, that the government of this country is not treating this house right or treating the people of this country as they should be treated. The hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) read a number of quotations from what some hon. members of parliament said with regard to the adjournment in 1926. They show conclusively that the present Prime Minister, who no doubt is more responsible for asking for this long adjournment than anyone, in 1926 fought with all the vigour he could against a long adjournment. It does not make any difference what the reason was, the fact is that the present Prime Minister fought against it. Not only did he, but Sir Henry Drayton had this to say:
Certainly before this motion should ever pass, the house ought to know what this government intends to do in the vacation.
Now we would like to know what this government intends to do in this vacation. It is not enough for them to say that the Prime Minister is going to the jubilee and they want to wait until he comes back. It is not enough to say, as the Minister of Justice said, that they want to bring in legislation following the report of the price spreads commission, because that legislation could have been ready long before this. Sir Henry Drayton said about the government of that day, we should know how this broken-up, broken-down government is to be reconstructed. I say that the reason for this adjournment is to try by some sleight-of-hand method to reconstruct this government and its policy before they go to the country. They realize that the radio addresses of the Prime Minister of January last fell flat; in my opinion and in the

opinion of many the Prime Minister is a poor politician-he should have held these speeches back until he was ready to come to parliament with some question on which he could force dissolution so that he could go to the country on it. But instead of doing that he gave himself away in these speeches which he made over the radio, with the result that the people of the country do not take any stock either in his promises or his dealt-bed performances.

speechtext:
He does not believe in
playing party politics.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO PROLONGED ADJOURNMENT EXPRESSED IN AMENDMENT TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member was nominated as a Tory a few days ago, was he not? The Prime Minister can play party politics just as well as you or I. Anyone who says the Prime Minister does not play party politics is not fair to him. If there is anything at which the Prime Minister is adept it is that.
Sir Henry Drayton also said:
We have wasted, if this adjournment is to take place, practically a month's time discussing an issue [DOT]which my hon. friends opposite now say they are incompetent to handle, and they must have six week's' time with a view to seeing whether the dead bones can again be made to function.
That is certainly very applicable to this government, because if ever there was a government of dead bones, this government, members of which made all the promises they did in 1930 and did not carry them out, is dead from the heels up.
The government should not ask us to vote for this adjournment. The government should carry on and get through with its business. I have no hesitation in saying that all over the country the expectation was that we should of course adjourn for a day or two at Easter, but we should not have to adjourn for six weeks. Is it fair to you and to me, Mr. Speaker, who came here in January thinking of course that with the "ability" of the Prime Minister and his colleagues they would go on with the business and get through the session at the earliest possible moment? We never anticipated any such proposals as this. We rented apartments, agreeing to pay a large sum of money per month to the end of the session; now if this adjournment takes place it means that scores of members of this house have to pay rent for their apartments and for electric light and telephones during the six weeks' adjournment. I say that is not fair to members of this house. The government have no right to ask the house to await the drafting of legislation arising out of the report of the price spreads commission, because my hon.

Long Adjournment-Mr. Blair
friends could have it ready to-morrow morning; anyway when the bill does come down it will be found that there is not a great deal in it. My hon. friends are certainly not going to the country with a lot of legislation about price spreads which is going to lose them more votes than they are going to lose anyway.
This country is in such a condition that there should not be an adjournment. I have word from different parts of the country that they want the business of the government carried on. The trouble is that we are not only sick in the body politic but the country is sick economically. My hon. friends made certain promises to this country. There is a man named Heinz who makes pickles of 57 different varieties, and they are mostly good, but the same cannot be said of the 68 different variety of promises made by the Prime Minister in the election of 1930, and which he has not endeavoured to carry out The people have waited for five years and they now demand that the government go to the country in order that business may be stabilized and that they may know what government they are going to have for the next five years.
I said a moment ago that this country is sick in the body politic and the body economic. We heard something about bulletins. I am going to refer to a bulletin which has come to me recently in regard to the health of this country. It says that the country is in very bad shape, it is in a neurotic condition, it has paralysis of peristalsis-

Not only has this country paralysis of peristalsis; it also has cataleptic paraplegia, due to promises made by the Prime Minister which were never carried out.

It means that the country's trade is paralyzed. When this government took charge in 1930 we had 82,500,000,000 worth of foreign trade. Under this Tory government in the last four years that has decreased to 8800.000,000. That is paraplegia, if my hon. friend the doctor from North Renfrew does not know what it means. This country has lost most of its trade, and this bulletin,
which I am going to give the acting Prime Minister so that he can consult his colleagues about it, says the country also has coronary thrombosis. The trade of the nation has gone down so far that the blood of the nation is not flowing freely, and it is suffering from stagnation due to the policies of this government. The bulletin also says the country has icterus.

subtopic: OBJECTION TO PROLONGED ADJOURNMENT EXPRESSED IN AMENDMENT TO MOTION FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: What is that?
